newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya eyes Middle East as new perishables market.
newsitem.headline: Kenya eyes Middle East as new perishables market.

text.p: Kenya's horticulture industry is increasingly eyeing the wealthy Middle East markets of the U.A.E. and Saudi Arabia as potential importers of the country's large volumes of fresh produce, traders and officials said on Friday.

Micah Cheserem, governor of the Central Bank of Kenya, urged producers, traders and industry officials to develop the potential for increasing exports of fruits and vegetables into the key markets in Saudi Arabia, Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

"Your board should make it one of its key objectives to put maximum effort into open up new markets in the countries of the Middle East and the Far East," Cheserem told the Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya (FPEAK).

Cheserem was speaking about the importance on the Kenyan economy of the country's fast growing horticulture sector, and said the government would continue to support the "impressive growth" seen in the industry over the past five years.
Almost the entire Kenyan production of flowers, fruits and vegetables, which came to almost 85,000 tonnes worth $240 million in expert earnings in 1996, are shipped out of Nairobi as air cargo.

Some 90 percent of total fresh produce is transported by air, mostly to the European markets of Holland, the U.K., France and Germany, which account for 86 percent of Kenya's horticulture exports. Only 2.9 percent goes to the Middle East.

"We are now exploiting these new markets and the Middle East especially is coming up very well. They have to import all the fruit they eat and at the moment the imports from Africa are very minor," said Simon Ethangatta, chairman of FPEAK.
"We have a lot of flights going between Nairobi and Dubai and over the next few years we expect to see exports to the Middle East increase by at least 15 percent," Ethangatta told Reuters.
He said the FPEAK over the last year had sent several trade missions to the Gulf States in order to establish more contacts between traders and exporters associations.

All the major Gulf carriers fly to Nairobi, many of them with additional stops in other East African capitals, and several airlines, including Gulf Air and Emirates, have within the past six months increased route frequency.

"In the Middle East there is a big consumption of fresh produce, especially in Dubai where they are very interested in mangos. European markets are almost saturated and becoming more regulated and protectionist. Freight rates despite a downward trend are still high and space is getting harder to find.

"The Middle East is much closer but like Europe, enjoys a high standard of living and, because of the scarcity of water cannot produce very much fresh produce," said Gordon Burr, speaking on behalf of COLEAPC.

According to figures provided by COLEAPC, an independent association promoting the trade of horticulture products from 70 African, Pacific and Caribbean (APC) countries, the Middle East has in recent years increased imports of fresh produce.
"From 1991 to 1994 the UAE imports of fresh fruit and vegetables have increased by 40 percent in value to 1.2 million tonnes worth some $450 million.
"From 1991 to 1994 the Saudi Arabian imports of fresh fruits and vegetables have increased by 12 percent in value to 1.4 million tonnes worth slightly over $400 million," it said.
But of the total imports of fruits and vegetables to the UAE only three precent came from Africa while for Saudi Arabia African imports only accounted for 11 percent.

"There is still a lot of room for growth. In addition fresh fruit and vegetables are also used in very large volumes in the area because of a tradition of over catering and because alcohol is not used much," Burr said.

"Transport costs are a major factor in the competition for markets and Kenya's proximity to the Middle East...gives Kenyan exporters a big advantage over their Southern African and South American rivals," he said.
Burr said the "most significant markets" were the UAE and Saudi Arabia, with Dubai being the major air transport hub in the Gulf region.
"Produce consumption is increasing in UAE because of increasing wealth, increasing population and the growth in tourism," he said.

However, he warned Kenyan exporters to "carefully check potential customers and build business gradually until trust is established" as payment difficulties may occur when dealing with some Middle East markets.

"The market there is a bit difficult, you have to be careful about who you deal with. That's why we have been making a lot of trade missions there to establish good contacts. But every time we have been there with a mission we have got a lot of interest," FPEAK's Ethangatta said. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax+5017
